The main difference between a 2-stroke and a 4-stroke engine is the number of strokes (or cycles) that the piston makes in one complete rotation.

A 2-stroke engine completes a power cycle in two strokes of the piston, or two revolutions of the crankshaft. It consists of two stages: intake and power. In the intake stroke, a mixture of air and fuel is drawn into the cylinder through a transfer port. In the power stroke, the mixture is ignited by a spark plug, causing the piston to move downward and rotate the crankshaft. The exhaust port then opens, allowing the exhaust gases to escape. The cycle then repeats.

A 4-stroke engine, on the other hand, completes a power cycle in four strokes of the piston, or four revolutions of the crankshaft. It consists of four stages: intake, compression, power, and exhaust. In the intake stroke, a mixture of air and fuel is drawn into the cylinder through an intake valve. In the compression stroke, the intake valve closes, and the piston compresses the mixture. In the power stroke, the spark plug ignites the mixture, causing the piston to move downward and rotate the crankshaft. In the exhaust stroke, the exhaust valve opens, allowing the exhaust gases to escape. The cycle then repeats.

The main advantages of a 2-stroke engine are its simplicity, lightweight, and high power-to-weight ratio. However, it produces more emissions and requires a separate system to handle the unburned fuel and oil. A 4-stroke engine, on the other hand, is more complex, heavier, and has a lower power-to-weight ratio, but it produces fewer emissions and requires less maintenance.
